newsitem.title: USA: CJD deaths in U.S. rare, no tie to madcow -- CDC.
newsitem.headline: CJD deaths in U.S. rare, no tie to madcow -- CDC.

text.p: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said Wednesday that deaths from Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) were very rare in the United States and are not known to be linked to "mad cow" disease.

Asked about press reports that a 62-year-old Indiana man had died of CJD, which has been called the human version of "mad cow" disease, CDC spokesman Tom Skinner said about 200 people die from the disease in the United States each year but the variant of CJD linked to "mad cow" had not been found.
"If this person died of CJD, it is a rare instance but not unknown," Skinner said.
"We have not seen the new variant form of CJD" linked to "mad cow" by reports last year from Britain, he said.
Mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), sparked a consumer panic when a new strain of CJD in Britain was linked to BSE in British cattle.
No case of BSE has ever been detected in the United States cattle herd, Skinner said.
